title: TC2-33404
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellants are appealing a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that denied their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), his wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant) and their son, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Minor Appellant) are citizens of Mexico (collectively the Appellants). The Appellants are appealing a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that denied their claims for refugee protection.

The Appellants fear a man by the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX), and the Los Zetas cartel they allege he is associated with. They allege that XXXX and Los Zetas want to harm the Appellants out of revenge for the Principal Appellant filing a complaint against XXXX, that ultimately led to his imprisonment for XXXX years. The Principal Appellant filed a complaint after XXXX and others stole XXXX and other property from the Principal Appellant's father's XXXX.
The RPD decided that the Appellants have an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) - a safe location that is reasonable to relocate to - in Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas.
The Appellants submit that the RPD erred by deciding they have an IFA. They submit that XXXX and Los Zetas have the means and motivation to locate them anywhere in Mexico.
It is my decision that the RPD correctly decided that the Appellants have an IFA, and that they are therefore not entitled to refugee protection.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention1 refugees nor persons in need of protection. BACKGROUND The Appellants' Allegations

The following paragraphs are a summary of the Principal Appellant's narrative to his Basis of Claim form, and do not necessarily represent my findings of fact. The Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant rely on the Principal Appellant's narrative.

On XXXX XXXX, 2013, the Principal Appellant's father was assaulted, robbed and threatened by four subjects that were wearing ski masks waiting for him at his XXXX in XXXX, Hidalgo. They tied the father up, and confined him to a room while one of the subjects watched him. Two vans and a truck eventually arrived and took the father's XXXX and XXXX. They also stole the father's gun, watch, television, and his wallet.

The father asked the man who was watching him if he could use the bathroom. The man untied him, and when he returned to the bathroom the man did not do a good job of tying him back up. When the man left to go help the others load the XXXX, the Principal Appellant's father was able to get loose and escape the house.

The father went to a neighbour's house at a XXXX nearby and told them what had happened. The neighbour drove the father back home, first stopping at the father's brother's house to inform him what had happened.
The Principal Appellant's father arrived home at approximately 3am, and he notified the authorities. The authorities came to investigate the scene.

On XXXX XXXX, 2013, the Principal Appellant and his father went to the public ministry to file a report in the city of XXXX, Hidalgo. The Principal Appellant was a XXXX XXXX and had knowledge of Mexican laws, and he focused with the prosecutor on bringing justice for what had happened to his father.
On XXXX XXXX, 2013, a detention order was issued against XXXX, one of the men that participated in the robbery.
On XXXX XXXX, 2014, XXXX was sentenced to XXXX years for the offences of aggravated assault and organized crime. On XXXX XXXX, 2014, the Superior Court of Justice upheld the sentence.

After XXXX went to jail, the Principal Appellant and his father began receiving death threats for having participated in the criminal trial against XXXX. The first week of XXXX 2014, the Principal Appellant received a call from an unknown number. The unidentified caller asked for the Principal Appellant, and told the Principal Appellant that he had a big price to pay for putting him in jail and for the Principal Appellant to wait until he was out. The Principal Appellant hung up. The caller called again after a few minutes, but the Principal Appellant did not answer. The Principal Appellant told his mother and father not to answer any private calls. The unknown calls continued, but they were not answered.
Between 2015 and 2016, the Principal Appellant received four anonymous letters indicating, "You will regret putting me in jail."
In the third week of XXXX 2016, the Principal Appellant's father received a note that said, "You better cooperate," along with the head of a lamb at the door of his XXXX.

The Principal Appellant was very afraid and began to look for options to live in another state. The Associate Appellant was offered a job in Mexico City, and the Appellants went to live there in XXXX 2016.

At the beginning of 2017, the Principal Appellant's father notified the Principal Appellant by phone that he continued to receive phone calls warning that the Principal Appellant would be found to settle accounts. The Principal Appellant decided to look for another city to protect himself from the organized crime and from the Los Zetas cartel.

In mid-2017, the Principal Appellant received threats once again, but more aggressively. These threats were also against the Principal Appellant's family since the Principal Appellant and Associate Appellant were now married, and the Associate Appellant was pregnant. In these threats, they would say, "Be careful with your wife and child." The Principal Appellant was alarmed when he also started to receive calls from Los Zetas asking for money on a monthly basis from the Principal Appellant and his father.
Things appeared to calm down for some time, and at the beginning of 2018, the Principal Appellant spoke to the Associate Appellant about returning to XXXX to be closer to family.
In XXXX 2018, the Appellants returned to XXXX, and the atmosphere was very heavy with payments to Los Zetas and the constant threats from XXXX.
In mid-XXXX 2018, the Principal Appellant applied for a passport, and he received it on XXXX XXXX, 2018. The Principal Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018.

The Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant remained in Mexico, and lived with the Associate Appellant's brother in Pachuca, Hidalgo. The Associate Appellant worked at a XXXX office in Tulancingo, Hidalgo.
The Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2019. The RPD decision
The following paragraphs are a summary of the RPD decision, and do not necessarily represent my findings of fact.

The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's evidence was generally consistent and credible in relation to his experiences in Mexico prior to the Appellants' departure. The RPD noted that the Appellants delayed departing Mexico for a protracted period of time after they returned to XXXX after having relocated to Mexico City, where they had lived without facing serious physical harm for over a year before they concluded that they could return in safety to XXXX. The RPD further noted that the Appellants delayed claiming protection in Canada for a year and a half after arriving in Canada despite claiming to face serious harm in Mexico. However, the RPD did not make any adverse credibility findings, concluding that the Appellants' credibility was not a central determination of their claims given the RPD's finding that the Appellants have a viable IFA available to them.

The RPD found that the threat of harm to the Appellants is related to purely criminal activity on the part Los Zetas, namely the Appellants' claims relating to the thefts at the family XXXX and extortion at the hands of Los Zetas motivated by their desire to raise money. The RPD determined there was no nexus to the Convention refugee definition, and the RPD therefore assessed the claims under section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act2 (IRPA).
The RPD found that the Appellants have a viable IFA available to them in Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas.

The RPD found that it had not been established on a balance of probabilities that the Appellants would face a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture if they were to return to Mexico and relocate to Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas. The RPD found that the Appellants remained in Mexico for years after the robbery without facing serious physical harm, and that XXXX or Los Zetas feared by the Appellants do not have a continued interest in causing serious harm to them. In reaching these findings, the RPD noted that the Principal Appellant and his family faced no serious physical harm by those who committed the robbery or persons associated with Los Zetas after the robbery. The RPD found that any threat of harm to the Appellants would be further reduced given the passage of time since they left Mexico.

The RPD further noted that the Appellants relocated to Mexico City where they faced no serious physical harm during the year that they lived there, before returning to XXXX. The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's father, who owned the XXXX when it was robbed and continues to live in Mexico has faced no serious physical harm despite remaining in the immediate area of the XXXX since the robbery occurred in 2013. The RPD found that the Principal Appellant has never been a source of income to Los Zetas, and further that he has been outside Mexico for over four years.

The RPD considered the country condition evidence, and found, among other things, that Los Zetas has been largely decimated in Mexico, with its remnants being fragmented, and that generally their power and influence has greatly diminished since its height in the mid-2010s. The RPD found that given the fragmentation of Los Zetas, that the remnants of Los Zetas lack the organizational strength or capability to pursue the Appellants or cause serious harm to them in the IFA locations.

The RPD found that the evidence does not establish that XXXX or persons associated with him or what remains of Los Zetas would be sufficiently motivated to expend time, energy and resources in attempts to cause serious harm to the Appellants if they were to return to Mexico and relocate to Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas.

The RPD found that it is objectively reasonable in all circumstances, including the Appellants' particular circumstances, for them to relocate to Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas. The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's and Associate Appellant's educational and employment background in the XXXX professions would allow them to secure gainful employment in a variety of fields, and that the Minor Appellant and the Canadian-born child would have access to continuing education in Mexico. The RPD found that the Appellants would face no serious linguistic or physical impediments to relocating to Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas, and that the Appellants had not established that they will face serious social, economic or other barriers in relocating.

For the following reasons, I deny the Appellants' request to admit the following documents as new evidence: a. The Law on Transparency and Access to Public Information for the State of Hidalgo, and a certified English translation of Article 13 from page 11, which the Appellants submit confirms the requirement that local regional authorities ensure that the identities and contact information for all legal practitioners are made publicly available through statute.3
The IRPA anticipates that an appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) will ordinarily be based on the record of the RPD proceeding.

According to section 110(4) of the IRPA, I can only accept new evidence on this appeal that: arose after the RPD decision (the RPD issued its written decision on October 25, 2022); was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision; or, the Appellants could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision.

If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible (e.g., the source and the circumstances in which it came into existence) and relevant before I can accept it.4

The burden of establishing the admissibility of new evidence lies on the party submitting that evidence, and the party must provide full and detailed submissions on the admissibility and relevance of the proposed new evidence.5

The Appellants submit that this evidence was unavailable when their claim was heard and decided by the RPD and could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have been presented. The Appellants argue that the document was found "...after their hearing was heard on August 31, 2022...," and would have been relevant to the issue of IFA, particularly the determination of motive and means of the agent of harm.6

I am not persuaded by the Appellants' submissions. The applicable date in section 110(4) is the date of the RPD decision.7 The Appellants could therefore have requested to provide this document in question after the RPD hearing and before the RPD issued its decision given that the RPD hearing took place on August 31, 2022, and the RPD did not issue its decision until two months later on October 25, 2022.8 The Appellants have not explained why this document was not provided before the RPD decision.

The Appellants were required to put their best foot forward to the RPD, and in this case, this proposed document could and should have been provided to the RPD before its decision.9 The fact that the Appellants did not anticipate a negative RPD decision is not a basis for using the RAD appeal as an opportunity to remedy their evidentiary deficiencies.10

The Appellants have not established that they could not have provided the document sooner with reasonable effort. Waiting until one receives a negative RPD decision in order to conduct a better search for information afterwards, that should have been provided to the RPD in the first place, is simply an attempt to complete a deficient record and defeats the purpose of the rules around new evidence.11
I do not have discretion to admit the proposed documents as new evidence because the document does not meet the requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA.12 ORAL HEARING
For the following reasons, I deny the Appellants' request for an oral hearing.

The Federal Court has commented that an appeal of an RPD decision to the RAD is intended to be a paper-based appeal,13 and that holding an oral hearing is an exception:14 The scheme of the IRPA is that the RAD must proceed without conducting a hearing. The exception to this is where the new evidence meets the s 110(4) requirements; meets the implicit Raza criteria, which includes the credibility of the evidence (Singh at para 44 and 49); and, meets the requirements of s 110(6), being that the RAD is of the opinion there is documentary evidence that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.
Having not admitted any new evidence, I am required to determine this appeal on the merits without holding a hearing.15 ANALYSIS Internal Flight Alternative

I find that after correctly giving notice at the RPD hearing that an IFA would be an issue, and specifically that the proposed IFA locations were Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas,16 the RPD correctly decided that the Appellants have a viable IFA in those locations, and that they are therefore not entitled to refugee protection. IFA: General Principles

The Federal Court has explained the general principles for an IFA, and has indicated that to determine if a viable IFA exists, I must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that:17 a. there is no serious possibility of the Appellants being persecuted based on Convention grounds or subjected to, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture or a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA area; and b. in all the circumstances, including circumstances particular to the Appellants, conditions in the IFA are such that it would not be unreasonable for the Appellants to seek refuge there.

Both above "prongs" of the test must be satisfied to conclude that the Appellants have a viable IFA. The threshold on the second prong of the IFA test is a high one. There must be "actual and concrete evidence" of conditions that would jeopardize the Appellants' lives and safety in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area. Once the potential for an IFA is raised, the Appellants bear the onus of establishing it is not viable. First Prong: No risk of persecution or harm in Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas

For the following reasons, I find that there is no serious possibility of the Appellants being persecuted based on Convention grounds or subjected to, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture or to a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFAs of Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas.

The Appellants argue that XXXX and Los Zetas are motivated to inflict cruel and unusual treatment and harm, and kill them as revenge for filing a police report and pursuing a criminal case that resulted in the conviction and incarceration of XXXX.18 The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in concluding that the agents of harm lack the motivation to track them. They argue that the motive is clear, which is to hold the Principal Appellant and his father responsible for filing the police report and providing key evidence used in convicting and incarcerating XXXX.

The Appellants argue that XXXX motive is ongoing and indefinite, and that it is implausible that XXXX, without any evidence or explanation, would change his mind about the Appellants once they change geographic locations or with the mere passage of time. The Appellants argue that XXXX is due for release in 2023, and will be free to execute his revenge. The Appellants submit that Los Zetas is quite capable of tracking down enemies using different methods ranging from direct tracking to the use of information provided by corrupt authorities. The Appellants argue that they are both legal professionals and they would have to register their identities, credentials and contact details with the federal authority, which is national information that is public and can be used by anyone to locate any legal professional in Mexico.
I am not persuaded by the Appellants' submissions.

A distinction must be made between an agent of harm's ability to find someone, and their motivation to do so. The issue of motivation is important because if there is no motivation for the agents of harm to locate the Appellants in the proposed IFAs, then the agent's capacity to locate the Appellants there is not relevant.19 Justice McHaffie of the Federal Court explained as follows:20 It is important to note that there is a difference between a persecutor's ability to pursue an individual throughout a country and his desire to do so or interest in doing so. The fact that a persecutor is able to pursue an individual is not decisive evidence that he is motivated to do so. If the persecutor has no desire to find, pursue and/or persecute an individual, or interest in doing so, it is reasonable to conclude that there is no serious possibility of persecution.

I find that the alleged agents of harm, XXXX and Los Zetas, do not have the motivation to track the Appellants to the proposed IFAs. The agents of harm were not motivated to track the Appellants when they remained in XXXX, and relocated close by to Pachuca and Mexico City. There is a lack of evidence that the agents of harm would expend the time, effort and resources to track the Appellants to the proposed IFAs, two of which are a great distance away from XXXX. The proposed IFA of Merida is 1,313 kilometres away from XXXX. The proposed IFA of Cabo San Lucas is 1,869 kilometres away from XXXX. The third proposed IFA of Mexico City is only 98 kilometres away from XXXX, however, the Appellants moved to Mexico City previously and were safe while they were there.

As I will explain below, the reasons I find that the alleged agents of harm are not motivated to locate the Appellants outside of XXXX are: (a) the Appellants only received sporadic and idle threats when they were in XXXX after the robbery, which were never followed up with any contact or attempts to harm the Appellants; (b) the Appellants moved to Mexico City, just 98 kilometres away, and only near the end of their time there started receiving phone calls, which were never followed up with any contact or attempts to harm the Appellants; (c) these idle phone threats in Mexico City were not serious, as evidenced by the fact the Appellants decided to move from Mexico City back to XXXX, the place where the threats began; (d) the Appellants continued to receive sporadic and idle threats in XXXX that were never followed up with any contact or attempts to harm the Appellants; (e) the Principal Appellant left for Canada, and the Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant moved to Pachuca, only 38 kilometres away from XXXX, where they lived for over a year and during which time the idle threats were never followed up with any contact or attempts to harm the Appellants; (f) if Los Zetas, allegedly acting on behalf of XXXX, had the motivation to track the Appellants they could have easily done so while the Appellants remained in XXXX after XXXX sentence; when the Appellants moved to Mexico City, a short distance away; when the Appellants returned to XXXX; and then when the Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant relocated to Pachuca, also a short distance away.

The robbery of the Principal Appellant's father's XXXX in XXXX occurred in XXXX 2013. By XXXX 2013, XXXX had been detained for the crime. In XXXX 2014, XXXX was sentenced to XXXX years imprisonment, which was upheld by the superior court in XXXX 2014.
The Appellants continued to live in XXXX.

The Principal Appellant testified that after XXXX was sentenced, the threats began at the end of 2015. He testified that no money was ever paid to Los Zetas. The RPD member asked if any adverse consequences resulted, and the Principal Appellant testified that there were death threats, and that the calls were coming on behalf of XXXX. The RPD member asked the Principal Appellant how he knew that, and the Principal Appellant testified that in one of the calls the caller said the Appellants would pay very dearly for putting XXXX inside and that he has friends in the Los Zetas. The Principal Appellant testified that anonymous messages were received after that, and on one occasion there was a sheep head left on the doorstep of his father's XXXX.21
The Appellants continued to live in XXXX.

The Principal Appellant testified that he thought if the Appellants moved to Mexico City that maybe the agents of harm would forget about things over time, and would stop harassing him. He testified that the Associate Appellant was offered a job in Mexico City, so things all came together at the time and they decided to move.22
The Appellants moved to Mexico City in XXXX 2016. Mexico City is approximately XXXX kilometres from XXXX.

The Principal Appellant explained that the Appellants did not face any problems in Mexico City while they were there for almost a full year, but that the problems continued back in XXXX, Hidalgo, with his father continuing to receive calls and anonymous messages.23 The Principal Appellant then clarified that almost at the end of their time in Mexico City, he received calls. The Principal Appellant testified that he did not know how they found his new number, commenting that "criminal organizations have lots of resources, methods."24
The Principal Appellant indicated in his narrative that, "Things appeared to calm down for some time."25 The Appellants returned to XXXX in XXXX 2018.

The RPD member asked the Principal Appellant why he felt secure enough to go back to XXXX given the phone calls. The Principal Appellant testified:26 Well I had hoped, I mean I thought that you know it could be safe but the fact that having moved away for a time that maybe something had changed that they would stop looking for us that they would stop coming around the XXXX with vehicles to monitor that was my hope.
The Principal Appellant left Mexico for Canada in XXXX 2018.

The RPD member asked the Principal Appellant why he decided to leave the country shortly after returning to XXXX. He explained that shortly after they arrived back, his father felt like he was being followed and was seeing trucks going around the XXXX and house. He testified that they felt the situation was getting closer, "And I don't really know what the exact word to use, but we just kind of felt like at any moment they could pounce and that maybe they would grab me and kidnap me or kill me."27

The RPD member asked the Principal Appellant why he left Mexico for Canada before the Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant. The Principal Appellant explained that he was afraid and left with fear, but tried to leave his wife and child in a safe situation with her brother in a different municipality (Pachuca), hoping that the agents of harm would forget about them.28
The Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant went to live in Pachuca from XXXX 2018 to XXXX 2019. Pachuca is approximately 38 kilometres away from XXXX.

The Principal Appellant explained that the Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant were safe in Pachuca for a while, but then the threats started against the Minor Appellant.29 He explained that the threat commenced at approximately the beginning of 2019.30 Los Zetas never followed up with any contact or attempts to harm the Associate Appellant and Minor Appellant before they came to Canada in XXXX 2019.

I am not persuaded by the Appellants' argument that XXXX release from prison this year increases their risk of persecution or harm if they were to relocate to the proposed IFAs. The Appellants have alleged that Los Zetas has been acting on behalf of XXXX while he has been in prison. For the reasons I have set out above, I have found that Los Zetas has not been motivated to harm the Appellants even while they were in XXXX or close by in Mexico City and Pachuca during the years before they left for Canada.

The Appellants have not provided sufficient evidence to support a finding that XXXX release from prison would motivate Los Zetas to track the Appellants to the proposed IFAs, when Los Zetas was not motivated to track and harm the Appellants when the Appellants remained essentially right in front of them for years. The National Documentation Package (NDP) for Mexico addresses the motivation of cartels to target people. I could not find any evidence in the NDP that indicates that a cartel would significantly delay a longstanding opportunity to act on its alleged motivation to harm their alleged targets because they are waiting for the release of someone from prison. There is a lack of evidence to explain why XXXX being in prison prevented Los Zetas from acting on their alleged motivation to seek revenge against the Appellants, and it is speculative that XXXX release from prison after ten years will be the condition that will trigger Los Zetas to be motivated to track and harm the Appellants in the proposed IFAs.

I considered but am not persuaded by the Principal Appellant's testimony that XXXX family might pose a future risk to them if they were to relocate to the proposed IFAs. I find this assertion to be speculative. The Principal Appellant speculated that XXXX family would want to harm him. He admitted that he had never met any members of XXXX family, and speculated that, "No, what I wanted to say is that by virtue of the fact that they are his family members and the fact that he was jailed, his family would be upset by that. And so they would want to help him."31 However, he conceded that members of XXXX family had never actually threatened or caused harm to the Principal Appellant or any members of the Principal Appellant's family.32

I also find that the other criminals involved in the robbery do not pose a risk of harm to the Appellants in the proposed IFAs. The Principal Appellant testified that he never encountered any of the other criminals involved in the robbery.33

I am not persuaded by the Appellants' suggestion that they could not go to any of the IFAs because they would have to register their names in the public database of legal professionals. If the agents of harm are not motivated to find the Appellants, which I have found they are not, then the capability of finding the Appellants through the on-line publicly available database of XXXX professionals is not relevant.34 My reasoning is supported by the fact that the Appellants were not harmed while in Mexico City for over a year even though the Associate Appellant, who is a XXXX, was working and would have been in the on-line database of XXXX professionals during that time (the Appellants argue that it is a requirement to have one's information published in this database).

The Principal Appellant testified that one month prior to the RPD hearing, people in trucks were coming around and asking for the Principal Appellant.35 I find this may support that there is interest in the Principal Appellant if he were to return to XXXX, but it does not support that the agents of harm are motivated to pursue the Appellants outside of XXXX to the proposed IFAs.

In conclusion, the Appellants' subjective fear that they face more than a mere possibility of a section 96 risk, or, on a balance of probabilities, a section 97 risk in the proposed IFAs is not sufficient evidence to conclude that the Appellants do not have any IFAs. As Justice McHaffie of the Federal Court stated, "... the Maldonado presumption is simply that a sworn witness is telling the truth. It is not a presumption that everything the witness believes to be true, but has no direct knowledge of, is actually true."36 Justice Kane of the Federal Court stated that, "relying on a sworn statement and the presumption of truthfulness from Maldonado does not absolve a claimant from providing sufficient evidence to support their claim."37 Just because the Appellants state that they are fearful and believe that XXXX, Los Zetas or XXXX family will find them in the proposed IFAs, does not mean that those alleged agents of harm will be motivated to track them to the proposed IFAs. Subjective fear is not enough to establish a claim.38 Second Prong: Relocating to Merida, Mexico City or Cabo San Lucas is not unreasonable
I do not find any errors in the RPD's reasoning that the Appellants have not met the high threshold of showing that relocating to the IFAs is unreasonable.

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to establish that it would not be unduly harsh for the Appellants to move to another, less hostile part of Mexico before seeking refugee status abroad. They submit that they are both over 30 years old, and that adverse conditions of age discrimination exist which would jeopardize their lives and safety in relocating to the proposed IFAs. They submit that age discrimination in hiring practices is prevalent in Mexico, and that it will adversely affect the ability of the Appellants to settle, survive and take care of themselves. The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to provide an explanation impugning age discrimination in the IFA locations.

The Appellants also argue that they have limited family connections in the proposed IFA locations, and that the presence or absence of family in an IFA is a factor in assessing the reasonableness of an IFA.
I am not persuaded by these submissions. The Appellants have not met their onus of demonstrating that the IFAs are unreasonable.39

The Appellants have not provided sufficient evidence to support their argument that people in their 30s face age discrimination in employment in the proposed IFAs, particularly people with the Appellants' background, including their high level of education, work experience and no language impediments.40 The Federal Court has held that the threshold for objective unreasonableness is very high on the second prong of the IFA test, and poor job prospects or a high unemployment rate are not enough to render an IFA objectively unreasonable.41

The Appellants have not provided sufficient evidence to support their argument that the lack of family members renders the proposed IFAs unreasonable. The absence of family members would have to rise to the level of jeopardizing the Appellants' lives or safety before it could be said that the IFAs were unreasonable.42 Considering the Appellants' personal circumstances, it cannot be said that the absence of family members would jeopardize their lives or safety. For example, they are not ill, elderly, a minor or disabled, which may be factors that are more relevant to whether the lack of family members in the proposed IFAs would cause undue hardship.43

While there will be hardships with relocating, including finding a house and a job, such hardships of relocating and starting a new life do not meet the high threshold of unreasonableness, which requires nothing less than the existence of conditions that would jeopardize the lives and safety of the Appellants in travelling or relocating to the proposed IFAs.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
